{{Short description|Generalizations of <math>0</math> in algebraic structures}}
{{other uses of|Zero}}
{{RefImprove|date=August 2020}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''zero element''' is one of several generalizations of [[0|the number zero]] to other [[algebraic structure]]s. These alternate meanings may or may not reduce to the same thing, depending on the context.

==Additive identities==
An ''[[additive identity]]'' is the [[identity element]] in an [[Abelian group|additive group]] or [[monoid]]. It corresponds to the element <math>0</math> such that for all <math>x</math> in the group, <math>0+x=x+0=x</math>. Some examples of additive identity include:
* The '''zero vector''' under [[vector addition]]: the vector whose components are all <math>0</math>; in a [[normed vector space]] its norm (length) is also <math>0</math>. Often denoted as <math>\mathbf{0}</math> or <math>\vec{0}</math>.<ref>{{cite book
 | last1 = Nair | first1 = M. Thamban 
 | last2 = Singh | first2 = Arindama
 | year = 2018
 | title = Linear Algebra
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=WW1lDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA3
 | page = 3
 | publisher = Springer
 | isbn = 978-981-13-0925-0
 | doi = 10.1007/978-981-13-0926-7
| bibcode = 2018lial.book.....N 
 }}</ref>
* The '''zero function''' or '''zero map''' defined by <math>z(x)=0</math>, under [[Pointwise|pointwise addition]] <math>(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)</math>
* The ''[[empty set]]'' under [[Union (set theory)|set union]]
* An ''[[empty sum]]'' or ''empty [[coproduct]]''
* An ''[[Initial and terminal objects|initial object]]'' in a [[category (mathematics)|category]] (an empty coproduct, and so an identity under [[coproduct]]s)

==Absorbing elements==
An ''[[absorbing element]]'' in a multiplicative [[semigroup]] or [[semiring]] generalises the property <math>0\cdot x=0</math>. Examples include:
*The ''[[empty set]]'', which is an absorbing element under [[Cartesian product]] of sets, since <math>\varnothing\times S=\varnothing</math>
*The '''zero function''' or '''zero map''' defined by <math>z(x)=0</math> under [[Pointwise|pointwise multiplication]] <math>(f\cdot g)(x)=f(x)\cdot g(x)</math>
Many absorbing elements are also additive identities, including the empty set and the zero function. Another important example is the distinguished element <math>0</math> in a ''[[field (mathematics)|field]]'' or ''[[ring (mathematics)|ring]]'', which is both the additive identity and the multiplicative absorbing element, and whose [[principal ideal]] is the smallest ideal.

==Zero objects==
A ''[[zero object]]'' in a [[category (mathematics)|category]] is both an [[Initial and terminal objects|initial and terminal object]] (and so an identity under both [[coproduct]]s and [[Product (category theory)|products]]). For example, the trivial structure (containing only the identity) is a zero object in categories where morphisms must map identities to identities. Specific examples include:
*The ''[[trivial group]]'', containing only the identity (a zero object in the [[category of groups]])
*The '''zero module''', containing only the identity (a zero object in the category of [[module (mathematics)|modules]] over a ring)

==Zero morphisms==
A ''[[zero morphism]]'' in a [[category (mathematics)|category]] is a generalised absorbing element under [[function composition]]: any morphism composed with a zero morphism gives a zero morphism. Specifically, if <math>0_{XY}:X\to Y</math> is the zero morphism among morphisms from <math>X</math> to <math>Y</math>, and <math>f:A\to X</math> and <math>g:Y\to B</math> are arbitrary morphisms, then <math>g\circ 0_{XY}=0_{XB}</math> and <math>0_{XY}\circ f=0_{AY}</math>.

If a category has a zero object <math>0</math>, then there are canonical morphisms <math>X\to 0</math> and <math>0\to Y</math>, and composing them gives a zero morphism <math>0_{XY}:X\to Y</math>. In the [[category of groups]], for example, zero morphisms are morphisms which always return group identities, thus generalising the function <math>z(x)=0</math>.

==Least elements==
A ''[[least element]]'' in a [[partially ordered set]] or [[Lattice (order)|lattice]] may sometimes be called a zero element, and written either as <math>0</math> or <math>\bot</math>.

==Zero module==
In [[mathematics]], the '''zero module''' is the [[module (mathematics)|module]] consisting of only the additive [[identity element|identity]] for the module's [[addition]] function. In the [[integer]]s, this identity is [[0 (number)|zero]], which gives the name ''zero module''. That the zero module is in fact a module is simple to show; it is closed under addition and [[multiplication]] trivially.

==Zero ideal==
In [[mathematics]], the '''zero ideal''' in a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>R</math> is the [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] <math>0</math> consisting of only the additive identity (or [[0 (number)|zero]] element). The fact that this is an ideal follows directly from the definition.

==Zero matrix==
{{Main|Zero matrix}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly [[linear algebra]], a ''[[zero matrix]]'' is a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] with all its entries being [[0 (number)|zero]]. It is alternately denoted by the symbol <math>O</math>.<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Lang | first = Serge | authorlink = Serge Lang
 | title = Linear Algebra
 | year = 1987
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=0DUXym7QWfYC&pg=PA25
 | series = [[Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics]]
 | page = 25
 | publisher = Springer
 | isbn = 9780387964126
 | quotation = We have a zero matrix in which <math> a_{ij} = 0 </math> for all <math> i, j </math>. ... We shall write it <math> O </math>.}}</ref> Some examples of zero matrices are

:<math>
0_{1,1} = \begin{bmatrix}
0 \end{bmatrix}
,\ 
0_{2,2} = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
,\ 
0_{2,3} = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
,\ 
</math>

The set of ''m'' × ''n'' matrices with entries in a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''K'' forms a module <math>K_{m,n}</math>.  The zero matrix <math>0_{K_{m,n}}</math> in <math>K_{m,n}</math> is the matrix with all entries equal to <math>0_K</math>, where <math>0_K</math> is the additive identity in ''K''.  

:<math>
0_{K_{m,n}} = \begin{bmatrix}
0_K & 0_K & \cdots & 0_K \\
0_K & 0_K & \cdots & 0_K \\
\vdots & \vdots &  & \vdots \\
0_K & 0_K & \cdots & 0_K \end{bmatrix}
</math>

The zero matrix is the additive identity in <math>K_{m,n}</math>. That is, for all <math>A \in K_{m,n}</math>:

:<math>0_{K_{m,n}}+A = A + 0_{K_{m,n}} = A</math>

There is exactly one zero matrix of any given size <math>m\times n</math> (with entries from a given ring), so when the context is clear, one often refers to ''the'' zero matrix. In a [[matrix ring]], the zero matrix serves the role of both an additive identity and an absorbing element. In general, the zero element of a ring is unique, and typically denoted as <math>0</math> without any subscript to indicate the parent ring. Hence the examples above represent zero matrices over any ring.

The zero matrix also represents the [[linear transformation]] which sends all vectors to the zero vector.

==Zero tensor==
In [[mathematics]], the '''zero tensor''' is a [[tensor]], of any order, all of whose components are [[0 (number)|zero]]. The zero tensor of order <math>1</math> is sometimes known as the zero vector.

Taking a [[tensor product]] of any tensor with any zero tensor results in another zero tensor. Among tensors of a given type, the zero tensor of that type serves as the additive identity among those tensors.
